items.title: Vegas turns to Adin Hill after Carter Hart exits morning skate with injury
items.desc: Vegas Golden Knights goalie Carter Hart left the team's morning skate with an undisclosed injury. Adin Hill will start Tuesday night's game against the Ottawa Senators.

stories.take:
Per ESPN, Vegas goalie Carter Hart left Tuesday's morning skate with an undisclosed injury, and Adin Hill will start against the Ottawa Senators instead. The Athletic's Jesse Granger posted that Hart "went down awkwardly, then limped off the ice here at morning skate."

Hill is a fair bet to hold the net, but neither goalie has been good so far this season. Our goals saved above expected, which measures how many goals a goalie stopped compared with what the quality of shots would predict, has Hill at -2.36 over five games (.882 save percentage) and Hart at -0.72 over eight (.889). Hill's -15.02 last season in 27 games is a reason for caution. The cost to VGK is real, since the team has been strong in front of its goalies, with 56.4% of the expected goals (the quality of chances, summed up) and 54% at five-on-five, yet its goaltending sits at -3.3 as a team. A goalie swap alone won't fix that. OTT, at 51.7% of expected goals, has had decent goaltending (+1.5), so this is a game where Vegas's edge in play could be eaten by whoever is in the crease.

Kindel went 17 goals and 35 points in 77 games last year, and so far this season he has two goals and four points in nine games. His own expected goals (the quality of his shots and chances) come to 2.45, so he is about half a goal short of where his looks say he should be. That's a small sample and not much of a concern. The bigger flag is his 5-on-5 share of expected goals at 49 percent, with PIT's share running about 6 points better when he's off the ice. Pittsburgh as a whole sits 5-6-1, but at 5-on-5 the team controls 54 percent of the chances, and goaltending has saved 2.4 goals more than expected. Kindel is a 19-year-old picked 11th overall who put up 99 points in 65 WHL games, so his early two-way numbers matter less than whether the legs and the shot are back. We'd watch his first few games closely.

The Athletic reports that MSG Sports is splitting the Knicks and Rangers into separate publicly traded companies, with James Dolan staying on as CEO and executive chairman of both. It's a corporate restructuring, not a hockey move, and nothing in the report touches the roster or the coaching staff.

What the Rangers' numbers say is that the team on the ice looks solid, if unspectacular. NYR sit at 7-6-1 with 15 points through 14 games. Their share of expected goals, which measures the quality of chances each side creates, is 51.7 percent so far this season, a slight edge over their opponents. At five-on-five it's 52 percent. Their goals total is 1.4 below what those chances should have produced, and their goalies have saved 0.5 more than expected, so luck isn't flattering or hurting them much. The record is about what the play deserves. The power play generates 0.65 expected goals per game, and the penalty kill allows 0.54, a decent balance. Whatever happens upstairs, the question for NYR is still the same: can that small edge in chance quality hold over a full season?

The Flyers lose a top-pair defenseman who plays 17.35 minutes a night, though the numbers suggest his results were running ahead of his play. In four games so far this season he has one goal against an expected total of 0.33 (expected goals measure the quality of chances), and the team controlled only 30.49 percent of the expected goals at five-on-five when he was on the ice. PHI's share of the chances was 8.85 points better without him. That is a small sample, but it fits a team that sits at 3-7-3 and has 40.5 percent of the expected goals overall. The thin spot is at five-on-five, where PHI is at 38 percent. Goaltending has kept them afloat, saving 6.3 goals more than expected. Going by how the coach has used his players, Nick Seeler, at 20:05 a night, is next in line for Ristolainen's minutes. That is a projection, not a record of games already played without him.

Our numbers say the Red Wings captain is playing better than his stat line shows. Larkin has two goals and six points in 10 games so far this season, but his own expected goals (the quality of his shot chances) come to 3.03, about one goal more than he has scored. At 5-on-5 Detroit has generated 56.3% of the expected goals with him on the ice, and the team's share runs 2.58 percentage points better with him than without. He's playing 21.69 minutes a night, and our model has him at 1.08 expected goals per 60. That's a small sample, but the process points to a scorer who is due, not one in decline, after a 34-goal, 67-point season last year. For a buyer, that means paying for a top-line center whose results should catch up to his chances. For fantasy owners, it's a reason to hold if he's available.

The goalie numbers are thin, so treat them gently. Postava stopped 87.5 percent of shots in his one game so far this season, and our goals saved above expected (how many goals a goalie prevented compared with an average one facing the same shots) put him at -0.01, essentially dead even. He wasn't the reason DET won, and he didn't cost them either. He came up as a free agent who was never drafted, after posting a .937 save percentage over 25 AHL games for the Grand Rapids Griffins in 2025-26. The team picture is more interesting. DET sits at 4-4-3 but controls 52.2 percent of expected goals, a measure of chance quality, and has been 7.9 goals worse than expected in finishing, which points to bad luck more than bad play. EDM is 8-2-1 on 14.1 goals above expected, and their goalies have been 8.7 goals below expected, so that record rests on shaky ground.

Sharangovich, the other party in the collision, is a steady piece for CGY. He has 4 points in 10 games and plays 16.32 minutes a night, with 2.38 expected goals against 2 actual, so his scoring is close to what his chances warrant. Calgary controls 50.47% of 5-on-5 expected goals with him on the ice, and the team's share rises 4.22 points when he plays, even as the Flames sit 4-6-0.

The rough night doesn't change the bigger picture for New York. So far this season the Rangers have created 51.9 percent of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality) and sit at 7-5-1. Their goalies have saved 3.6 goals more than expected, so the goaltending has been a real strength, which makes one bad period a small dent. Los Angeles is a different story. The Kings are 2-5-2 and have 46.6 percent of the expected goals, and they have scored 3.7 fewer goals than the chances would suggest. Their goalies have also been 3.6 goals worse than expected. A three-goal burst against Reimer fits a team whose results have trailed its play, though the underlying numbers still lean New York's way. We'd treat this as one game, not a verdict on Reimer or the Rangers' goaltending.

The Hurricanes haven't needed him to get started. At 9-2-2 with 20 points through 13 games, CAR owns 60.9% of the expected goals so far this season. Expected goals measures the quality of chances each side creates, so that share says Carolina has controlled play, and the 59% at five-on-five shows it isn't a special-teams mirage. The penalty kill is allowing just 0.52 expected goals per game, which makes it a strength. Our numbers also show goals scored running slightly below expectation (-0.4), so the results aren't flattering the team. If anything, they've been a touch light.

That makes Nikishin's return an addition to a team already playing well, not a rescue. We'd watch how quickly he settles back into the lineup after missing camp, and whether the penalty kill, already strong, gets deeper with him on the ice.

So far this season, our numbers say CGY is closer to that goal than a 4-6-0 record suggests. The Flames have taken 45.5% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality, not just shot counts), a below-even share but not a collapse, and 47% at five-on-five. That points to bad puck luck and shaky goaltending, not just a weak roster. The special teams look middling, at 0.43 power-play expected goals per game and 0.73 allowed per game on the penalty kill. If the goaltending steadies, this team should win more than it has, and the "competitive every night" line looks believable. Any trade-piece talk will land on a team that is better than its record, with only 10 games of data behind that read.

That is a big part of why MIN sits at 7-3-2 and holds 58 percent of expected goals overall. VAN, at 2-9-1, takes only 38 percent of the chances, so the crowd has a lot more to be upset about than one departure. Daniel Wagner of Pass it to Bulis posted that "the dead-eyed gremlin always has the puck," which is a fair summary of what the data shows.

stories.take:
The Athletic reports that Canadiens captain Nick Suzuki will be out 2-4 weeks with an upper-body injury, ending his ironman streak at 546 games, the second-longest active streak in the NHL. The Hockey News says the injury underlines Montreal's need to upgrade at center.

The numbers show why this hurts. So far this season, Suzuki has 12 points in 9 games and plays 21.78 minutes a night. He has scored 1.06 goals more than his expected goals (a measure of chance quality) of 3.94, so some of that production is running hot. Still, when he is on the ice at five-on-five, MTL controls 56.97% of the expected goals, and the team's share rises 5.71 percentage points with him out there. MTL's overall share is just 49.2%, with a 4-3-2 record, so he is propping up a team that is otherwise average at best.

With no games missed yet, this is a projection based on how the coach has used his players. Cole Caufield, at 19:26 a night, is next in line for Suzuki's minutes, and Oliver Kapanen, the busiest man on the second power-play unit, is the likeliest to move up to the first unit.

The fines are small, but the two players are not equals on the ice so far this season. Tkachuk has 15 points in 11 games for FLA, mostly assists (12), and his own expected goals (a measure of the quality of his chances) of 3.0 match his 3 goals exactly, so nothing about his production looks lucky. When he plays 5-on-5, FLA creates 60 percent of the expected goals, and the team's share improves by 10.5 percentage points with him on the ice. Cousins is a depth forward at 9.19 minutes a game, with 2 points. OTT's share of expected goals drops by almost 20 percentage points when he plays, and he sits at 36 percent at 5-on-5. Both teams are outscoring their chances poorly so far this season (FLA is 4.4 goals below expected, OTT 4.6), which suggests both records could improve if the finishing evens out.

moves.take: Dallas announced it placed forward Matt Duchene on long-term injured reserve, retroactive to Sept. 29, and recalled forwards Arttu Hyry and Colin Blackwell from Texas (AHL). Hyry, who kills penalties on the third line, has three goals this season, about 1.2 more than his chances would predict, and Dallas controls more of the chance quality when he plays at even strength. moves.take: Pittsburgh announced it has reinstated center Blake Lizotte from injured reserve. Pittsburgh's team share improves by about 10 percentage points when he plays. His return should take minutes back from Hendrix Lapierre, who is next in line at 11:11 a night.
